finding.claim: reset_password_loose uses loose == to compare the stored reset token with the attacker-supplied $token. A boolean true (e.g. from a JSON body) matches any non-empty stored token, and a NULL/empty stored token matches an empty or missing token, so the password can be reset with only the email. Conditional on caller input types and DB state; the caller is not in the repo.
finding.source: $token parameter of reset_password_loose (reset.php:2), assumed attacker-controlled via the reset request; $email and $new also assumed attacker-controlled
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw (reset.php:5-6) for the supplied email

trace.note: $token accepted with no type or string check
SELECT token FROM resets WHERE email = quoted $email; fetch() returns first row

finding.guards_checked: $db->quote() on email (no SQL injection); $row null guard present; no type check on $token; no hash_equals; no expiry check. Function is a legacy copy of reset_password; any remaining caller is exposed.

verdict.guard_found: Only the `$row` truthiness check at reset.php:4. No type check on `$token`, no hash_equals, no expiry check, and no caller in the repo to show who can reach reset.php:2. The sibling `reset_password` (reset.php:12-20) uses hash_equals and is not the flawed path.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: reset.php:4 uses loose `==` on the stored token, and reset.php:5-6 then updates the password for the supplied email, with no effective guard in the function. Whether an attacker can reach `reset_password_loose` at all depends on a caller that is not in this repo (the only file is reset.php), so exploitability cannot be decided from the code available.

finding.claim: Reset tokens are never consumed or expired. A successful reset leaves the resets row in place, and the lookup has no expiry or ORDER BY, so an old or leaked token can be replayed for repeated password changes.
finding.source: Any previously issued or leaked reset token for the email
finding.sink: Password update on successful token match (reset.php:5-6 and reset.php:15-16)

trace.note: SELECT token only; no expires_at/created_at check; no ORDER BY
same lookup in reset_password; only first row checked
success path in loose variant does not delete or mark token used
success path in strict variant does not delete or mark token used

finding.guards_checked: None in this file. Expiry or cleanup may exist elsewhere in the codebase, not visible here.

verdict.guard_found: none. reset.php:3 and reset.php:13 select only the token with no expires_at/created_at check and no ORDER BY. The success paths at reset.php:5-6 and reset.php:15-16 run an UPDATE on users and never delete or mark the resets row. The repo contains only reset.php, so no expiry job, token-issuance cleanup, or single-use check exists anywhere in the available code.
verdict.reason: The token lookups at reset.php:3 and reset.php:13 have no expiry filter, and the success paths at reset.php:5-6 and reset.php:15-16 never delete or invalidate the row, so a previously issued or leaked token keeps working after the victim has reset their password. The attacker only needs to possess a token already, so the impact is persistence after a leak rather than a fresh takeover; the cleanup-elsewhere caveat is moot because the repo has no other files.

finding.claim: reset_password accepts an empty token when the stored token is empty: hash_equals('', (string)null) is true. Conditional on a resets row with an empty token existing. A NULL stored token causes a TypeError (fatal), not a bypass.
finding.source: $token parameter of reset_password (reset.php:12), null or omitted yields '' after (string) cast

trace.note: lookup by quoted email, first row

finding.guards_checked: hash_equals (constant-time, correct primitive); $db->quote() on email; $row null guard. No rejection of empty token.

verdict.guard_found: none: reset.php:12-14 has no emptiness check on $token and no check on the stored token; the only control is hash_equals at reset.php:14, which returns true for two empty strings. The lookup at reset.php:13 is parameterized via $db->quote($email), and the null check at reset.php:14 only skips a missing row.
verdict.reason: The trace at reset.php:12-16 is accurate and an anonymous caller can pass an empty token (reset.php:12, 14), so a bypass exists whenever a resets row with an empty token exists; but the token-generation code that would create such a row is not in the available files, so reachability cannot be decided. The candidate's NULL-to-TypeError sub-claim is also wrong: in PHP 8.1+ a null passed to hash_equals (reset.php:14) is coerced to '' with a deprecation, so a NULL stored token is also a bypass rather than a fatal error.

finding.claim: Both reset functions return true without checking the result of $db->exec(), so a reset can be reported as successful when no users row matched the email or the write failed.
finding.sink: Return value of the reset functions (reset.php:7 and reset.php:17) after UPDATE at reset.php:5-6 and reset.php:15-16

trace.note: UPDATE executed via $db->exec with no return-value check

finding.guards_checked: None on the UPDATE result. Impact is a misleading success response, not a bypass.

verdict.guard_found: none. reset.php:5-6 and reset.php:15-16 run $db->exec() as a bare statement with its return value discarded, and reset.php:7 and reset.php:17 return true unconditionally. The only check is the token comparison at reset.php:4 and reset.php:14, which gates the UPDATE but does not verify that it changed a row. No exception mode is set in this file, so a failed exec() returns false silently.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: reset.php:5-7 and reset.php:15-17 discard the exec() result and return true, so a reset reports success when the UPDATE matches no users row (e.g. a resets row exists but users does not). The attacker is anyone holding a valid reset token, which they need anyway, so the impact is limited to a misleading success return value at reset.php:7 and reset.php:17, not a bypass or privilege gain; severity is low and depends on whether callers rely on the return value.

finding.claim: No password policy is enforced on $new (empty or arbitrarily short values are hashed and stored), and reset tokens are stored and read back in plaintext, so a database read exposes usable reset tokens.
finding.source: $new parameter (reset.php:2 and reset.php:12); stored token read at reset.php:3 and reset.php:13
finding.sink: password_hash($new) and UPDATE users SET pw (reset.php:5-6, reset.php:15-16); plaintext token read (reset.php:3, reset.php:13)

trace.note: password_hash applied to $new with no length or emptiness check
plaintext token selected from resets table

finding.guards_checked: password_hash with PASSWORD_DEFAULT is correct; email quoted via $db->quote(); no token logging in this file. Password policy and token hashing may exist elsewhere, not visible here.

verdict.guard_found: none. reset.php:5 and reset.php:15 call password_hash($new, PASSWORD_DEFAULT) with no length or emptiness check. reset.php:3 and reset.php:13 select the token from resets in plaintext, and reset.php:4 and reset.php:14 compare it directly (== in the loose variant, hash_equals in the other). The directory holds only reset.php, so no caller-side validation or token hashing is visible.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code: reset.php:3 and reset.php:13 read the reset token from the resets table in plaintext, and reset.php:5 and reset.php:15 hash $new with no policy check, so a reader of that table gets tokens that work directly against reset.php:4 or reset.php:14. The password-policy half is weak on its own, since a user only sets their own password, but the plaintext-token half is a real DB-read-to-account-takeover escalation with no effective guard in the visible code.
